blocks.content: PART A: BASIC CONCEPT OF POVERTY

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Poverty is a multi-dimensional issue extending beyond mere income deprivation to encompass social and economic factors.
Absolute Poverty refers to the lack of basic necessities for survival, whereas Relative Poverty reflects income inequality relative to others in society.
Individuals experiencing poverty can be categorized by duration into Chronic Poverty (persistently poor) and Transient Poverty (fluctuating in and out of poverty).
In India, the Poverty Line serves as the core benchmark for measuring poverty, primarily based on minimum calorie intake and private consumption expenditure.
Poverty alleviation strategies require a combination of high economic growth, direct government welfare interventions, and inclusive growth initiatives.

blocks.content: 1. Meaning of Poverty

Poverty refers to a condition in which a person does not have sufficient income or resources to meet the minimum requirements of life. These minimum requirements include food, clothing, shelter, education, healthcare and other basic necessities.
Thus, poverty is not merely lack of income. It also means lack of opportunities, poor living conditions, malnutrition, illiteracy and poor health.
2. Poverty as a Multi-Dimensional Problem
Poverty is a multi-dimensional problem because it affects economic, social and human development aspects. A poor person suffers from low income, poor health, lack of education and social exclusion.
3. Characteristics of Poverty

• Low income and low consumption

• Inability to meet basic needs

• Poor health and nutrition

• Low educational attainment

• Low productivity

• Social marginalisation
PART B: TYPES OF POVERTY (DETAILED CLASSIFICATION)
4. Absolute Poverty
Absolute poverty refers to a situation where a person’s income is insufficient to meet the minimum requirements for physical survival. It is measured using the poverty line.
If income or consumption falls below the poverty line, the person is considered absolutely poor.
5. Relative Poverty
Relative poverty refers to poverty in comparison with the average standard of living in society. Even if basic needs are met, a person may still be considered poor relative to others.
6. Chronic Poverty

Chronic poverty refers to poverty that persists for long periods or continues across generations. It is caused by structural factors such as illiteracy, lack of skills, landlessness and social discrimination.
7. Transient Poverty
Transient poverty is temporary poverty caused by short-term shocks such as natural disasters, crop failure, illness or economic slowdown.
PART C: POVERTY LINE (CORE  AREA)
8. Meaning of Poverty Line
Poverty line refers to the minimum level of income or consumption expenditure required to meet basic needs of life. People whose income or consumption falls below this line are considered poor.
9. Basis of Poverty Line in India
In India, the poverty line is based on minimum consumption expenditure rather than income. This approach considers food, clothing, housing, education and healthcare needs.
10. Methods of Measuring Poverty

1. Calorie Intake Method:

Minimum calorie requirement is fixed (rural and urban separately).



2. Consumption Expenditure Method:

Poverty line based on expenditure needed to meet basic needs.



3. Income Method:

Used mainly for international comparison.

rows: Condition where a household's income falls below the minimum needed to maintain basic living standards (food, shelter, water).
Condition where a household's income is significantly less than the average income of the surrounding economy.
Measured against a fixed threshold known as the Poverty Line.
Measured using income distribution metrics like the Gini Coefficient or Lorenz Curve.
Predominantly observed in developing and underdeveloped nations.
Present in all societies, including highly developed countries.

blocks.content: PART D: CAUSES OF POVERTY (EXPLAINED WITH LOGIC)
11. Economic Causes of Poverty

• Unemployment and underemployment reduce income

• Low agricultural productivity leads to low rural income

• Unequal distribution of income increases poverty

• Slow industrial growth limits job creation

• Inflation reduces purchasing power of poor
12. Social Causes of Poverty

• Rapid population growth

• Illiteracy and lack of skills

• Social customs and traditions

• Caste system and discrimination

• Gender inequality
PART E: EFFECTS OF POVERTY (DETAILED IMPACT)
13. Economic Effects of Poverty

• Low productivity due to poor health and education

• Low savings and investment

• Slow economic growth

• Inter-generational poverty trap
14. Social Effects of Poverty

• Malnutrition and poor health

• High illiteracy rate

• Crime and social unrest

• Poor quality of life
PART F: POVERTY ALLEVIATION MEASURES

items: Distinguish between Absolute Poverty (fixed minimum threshold for survival) and Relative Poverty (income inequality measure).
Understand the methodology and calorie/consumption standards used to determine the Poverty Line in India.
Identify the differences between Chronic Poverty (long-term poor) and Transient Poverty (seasonal or temporary poor) for exam questions.

blocks.content: 15. Role of Economic Growth
Sustained and inclusive economic growth is essential for poverty reduction as it creates employment and increases income.
16. Government Measures for Poverty Alleviation

• Employment generation programmes

• Public Distribution System

• Education and skill development schemes

• Social security measures

• Rural development programmes
17. Importance of Inclusive Growth
Growth must be inclusive so that benefits reach poor and vulnerable sections of society.
ABSOLUTE FINAL REVISION POINTS

• Poverty = inability to meet basic needs

• Poverty is multi-dimensional

• Absolute poverty measured by poverty line

• Relative poverty is comparative

• Poverty line based on consumption

• Poverty reduction needs growth + welfare
